definition: Abort means to give up on a half-finished project or effort.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word abort. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know abort should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When the crosswind gusted past the safety limit, the pilot chose to abort the landing and climb away for another circuit.
Pause is the gentlest stop, far short of abort — paused work waits a moment and then goes on where it left off, while an aborted effort is deliberately cut off mid-course, for good.
Shelve is milder than abort: a shelved project sits unfinished but alive, waiting for a better season, while an aborted one is ended for good, mid-course.

To scrap is to cancel something at any stage — even a plan still on the drawing board that nobody has begun. Abort is stricter: it ends an effort already underway, cut off mid-course on purpose. You can scrap what never started; you can only abort what is live.

To discontinue is to stop making or offering something, often winding it down gradually — a product line, a bus route. Abort is abrupt and mid-action: a live effort deliberately cut off at once. Discontinuing phases a thing out; aborting stops it dead.

Abort means to give up on a half-finished project or effort.
The mission director aborted the balloon launch at two minutes to release, with the envelope half filled, after the telemetry link dropped for the third time.

Abort is sharper than stop or cancel because it means ending an effort that is already underway — the launch had begun and was deliberately cut off mid-course, not merely rescheduled before it started.
Abort is the crisp word pilots, surgeons and engineers use for stopping something already in motion — an approach, a launch, a rollout.
It insists the effort was live and was ended mid-course, on purpose.
For casual plans, 'call off' sounds more natural, and scrap covers plans killed before they ever start — which abort, strictly, does not.

At the regional robotics finals, Priya's team had sixty seconds to run their machine through the obstacle course, and every point of their season rode on the attempt.
Twenty seconds in, she saw the left gripper sagging.
A servo was overheating, and every task ahead on the course needed that claw.
Her teammates shouted at her to push on, but Priya hit the red switch and aborted the run with the robot stalled at mid-course.
The rules allowed one restart per team.
A burned-out servo, she explained later, would have cost them the whole machine and the season -- not just the round.
They replaced the part in four minutes, ran again from the start, and finished second, with a robot still whole.
